question: The Swedish former minister and Social Democrat Ibrahim Baylan was appointed as a special adviser at EIT InnoEnergy in 20231. The financial newspaper Dagens industri later reported that Baylan was apparently an EU lobbyist for Harald Mix’s investment company Vargas, which was behind a number of outfits including Northvolt and H2 Green Steel, now known as Stegra2. Meanwhile, Bo Normark has been the head of industrial strategy at EIT InnoEnergy and an adviser at Vargas3. With the above in mind: 1.
Has the Commission looked into whether the overlapping roles at InnoEnergy, Vargas, Northvolt and Stegra have given rise to conflicts of interest or otherwise influenced decisions on EU funding?

Does the Commission take the view that it would be reasonable to exclude a company from EU funding when its managers or staff in other key positions have previously contributed – through negligence, mismanagement or irregularities – to the loss of EU or other public funds?

How does the Commission ensure that people who have been central to failed projects in receipt of large amounts of public funding are not able, without an in-depth review, to move on to new companies and projects that once again receive support or guarantees from EU taxpayers?

Nordic Projects, https://www.nordiskaprojekt.se/2023/02/28/eit-innoenergy-utser-ibrahim-baylan-tillny-särskild-rådgivare-2/. 2 Dagens Industri, https://www.di.se/nyheter/forre-s-toppen-blir-eu-lobbyist-at-harald-mix/. 3 Impact Loop, https://impactloop.se/artikel/decade-vaxer-med-nya-rekryteringar---tar-in-tunga-vargasrådgivaren. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The Commission places great importance in the prevention and management of conflict of interest (CoI) in the implementation of EU funds. InnoEnergy is a Knowledge and Innovation Community (KIC) designated by the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT).

The contractual relationship is between the EIT and InnoEnergy and it is therefore within the EIT’s competence to verify that all applicable grant conditions have been met. The Financial Regulation1 allows excluding entities from EU funding if specific exclusion grounds are established by a final judgement or through a preliminary classification in law by the early detection and exclusion system (EDES) panel.

Whether an entity should be excluded is assessed on a case-by-case basis, considering the specific circumstances. Where it is established that an entity’s misconduct constitutes grave professional misconduct - such as breaches of CoI rules - exclusion from EU funding is mandatory.

In this case, the EIT is responsible for the checks on InnoEnergy before and during the implementation of EU-funded activities, including checks to protect the EU’s financial interests. Where irregularities or exclusion grounds are found, the EIT takes the appropriate measures under the applicable rules.
The Commission is working on a revised EIT Regulation2 to be presented before the end of 2026, where it plans to propose stronger supervision of the KICs by the EIT.
